Variants.Content: Cologne stood on the Rhine as the largest city of the Holy Roman Empire, and its wealth came from river traffic, warehouses, and the pilgrims who came to see the relics of the Magi. Work on the cathedral began in 1248, and its vast choir was designed to hold the gilded Shrine of the Three Kings, made by Nicholas of Verdun. Pilgrims donated generously to the shrine, and that money fed the building's progress. The Archbishop-Elector held the title of Arch-Chancellor of Italy and sat among the men who chose the king of the Romans. He governed a city whose merchants guarded their charters jealously and whose council watched every toll and tax the archbishop tried to raise.

Patrician burghers kept challenging the prince-archbishop's feudal jurisdiction, and every court case over tolls or market rights became a contest for power. While the prelate counted electoral subsidies from foreign monarchs, the city council armed civic militias to guard its trade charters.
Floating timber rafts loaded with Mosel wine downriver means paying tolls at every abbey bend. But tying a three-crown pilgrimage pennant to the mast ensures bailiffs refrain from confiscating cargo.
